# Plain-language summary {.unnumbered #sec-plain}

Microcosm Dynamics is a computer model of Social Security's retirement, survivor and disability benefits that anyone can download, run and check. It follows individual Americans through time. In each simulated year, the people in the model can earn, marry, divorce, have children, become disabled, claim benefits and die. The model then applies Social Security's rules to each life to work out what that person collects. A model like this can answer questions that a snapshot of one year cannot, such as which retirees a benefit cut reaches decades from now.

Outsiders can read the results of the models that already do this work, including the Urban Institute's [DYNASIM](https://www.urban.org/research/publication/urbans-dynamic-simulation-income-model-4), the Social Security Administration's [MINT](https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/projections/methodology.html), the [Penn Wharton Budget Model](https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/model/social-security/) and the Congressional Budget Office's [long-term model](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/53667). CBO does not publish its model's code, and we found no public code with which to rerun DYNASIM, MINT or the Penn Wharton Budget Model. Among other models that estimate reforms across a population, we found public code for [OG-USA](https://github.com/PSLmodels/OG-USA) and the [Cato Institute's model](https://github.com/kchanwong/social_security_cato_model). We publish the [code](https://github.com/PolicyEngine/microcosm-dynamics), estimates and tests of Microcosm Dynamics under an open-source license.

Microcosm Dynamics is a work in progress. The end of this summary says what it cannot do yet and what we plan to add.

## Where the model's people come from {.unnumbered}

The model learns how lives unfold from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), a University of Michigan survey that has followed a set of American families, and the new families their members form, since 1968. It takes the ages at which people claim benefits from the Social Security Administration's published statistics. Every projection so far starts from PSID members, and all four comparisons below draw their people from the PSID. The model is also built to start from Microcosm, PolicyEngine's data on 166,302 people drawn mainly from the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey and weighted toward official totals, though no projection starts there yet.

The PSID's design limits what the model can learn from it. The survey interviewed 9,152 families in 2023, while the Current Population Survey samples about 95,000 households a year. Because it follows the 1968 families and their descendants, it covers later immigrants mainly through two small added samples. Of the original 1968 members still alive in 2015, about 40 percent were still responding, and those who left differ from those who stayed. Its records of low earnings have known measurement problems. Since 1997 it has interviewed every other year, and for the 7,486 people in the projections who reach age 62 between 1979 and 2030, about half of the career years through 2010 hold values we filled in or set to zero (@sec-psid).

## What we have tested it against {.unnumbered}

We test the model in two ways, first with pre-registered tests. Before we score a piece of the model, we post which statistics we will compare and how close counts as a pass. Each version of the piece then gets one scored run, against data set aside from what it learned from or data from outside sources, and we publish every result. We call these tests gates, a software-engineering term for the checks that code must clear before it ships. A piece that faces such a test joins the model only after it passes, though some pieces face no test yet.

The pieces that generate earnings, marriage and childbearing, work-limiting disability and who lives with whom each pass a pre-registered test, as does the step that applies the PSID's patterns to the people in Microcosm. A test run of the model's year-by-year projection, with its pieces running together, passes too: we let it learn from data through 2014 and compare its projected marriages, disability and earnings for 2015 to 2019 with what the PSID recorded. We had already seen the PSID's data for those years when we chose parts of the projection's design and the statistics that test compares. Four of the passes came only after a version failed and we publicly changed the test's terms: those for earnings histories, marriage and childbearing, the Microcosm step and the projection. In two of them, the version that passed is the same one that failed under the old terms.

The second way is four blind tests against published results from DYNASIM3, the previous generation of the Urban Institute's model. In each test, a separate workstream read DYNASIM3's published numbers twice, independently, and sealed them until we had saved the model's answer. The AI model that coordinated the build saw the cost-of-living test's values before that test ran, in a report that may also have held the retirement-age test's. The builders, some of them AI agents, could reach files of DYNASIM3 material, and the records cannot rule out that they opened them. Each test is blind only as far as those records show.

- **Cutting each year's cost-of-living adjustment by one percentage point.** By 2030 the cut lowers average benefits by about 4 to 18 percent in the model, and the model's change lands within 0.74 percentage points of DYNASIM3's in every age group. Once we choose the year from which each person's increases are cut, the cut's effect on benefits already being paid follows by arithmetic. The close match therefore says little about how well the model captures how lives change.
- **Raising the full retirement age, the age for an unreduced benefit, to 68.** For people aged 65 to 69 in 2030, the age group where the two models differ most, average benefits fall 5.7 percent in the model and 9.9 percent in DYNASIM3. In the other four age groups, the two models' changes lie within 1.09 percentage points of each other. The model leaves out changes in when people claim and the retirement earnings test, which withholds benefits from early claimants who keep working; either could account for the gap.
- **A 13 percent cut to every benefit.** For people born from 1936 to 1945, the poverty rate at age 67, on a measure that counts income people could draw from their wealth, rises 0.46 percentage points in the model and 2 points in DYNASIM3. The model's figure rests on 483 people born in odd years, so one person of average weight moves it by about 0.2 points. DYNASIM3's report rounds poverty rates to whole percentages, so its 2-point rise could lie anywhere between 1 and 3 points.
- **A minimum benefit tied to years of work.** Under the headline version, 7.75 percent of beneficiaries aged 62 and older receive the minimum in the model and 6.3 percent in DYNASIM3. Under the model's main assumptions, all four versions put a larger share of women and a smaller share of men on the minimum than DYNASIM3 does. Three of the six alternative assumptions we registered in advance break that pattern in at least one version.

DYNASIM3 is another model, so each gap measures a disagreement between two models, not an error in either. The first two tests project PSID families to 2030. The last two apply each reform to incomes people reported to the PSID. DYNASIM3's figures for those two come from projections published in 2004 and 2006, so part of each gap can reflect the different populations. None of the tests involves DYNASIM4, the current version, and none establishes that our model matches either version.

## What the model can and cannot say yet {.unnumbered}

The model can apply a reform to the incomes the PSID recorded and count whom it reaches. It can also take the 11,405 people born in 1980 or earlier in the families the PSID interviewed in 2011 and project them to 2030 under a reform, adding no newborns or immigrants. It reports how effects differ across people, such as benefit changes by age group and poverty at 67. It produces no cost estimates, no measure of Social Security's long-run balance and no date when the trust funds run out.

None of the four blind tests uses a piece that passes a pre-registered test. In the two 2030 projections, nobody earns, marries or divorces after 2010, and the benefit formula counts every year after 2010 as a year without earnings. A piece that projects earnings forward passes its own test, but neither projection uses it yet. The projections pay a retirement benefit to every claimant with earnings on record through 2010, without checking whether that person worked long enough to qualify. They do not yet apply the retirement earnings test, and nobody in them changes when they claim in response to a reform.

The parts that decide how long people live, when they claim, who receives disability insurance and who immigrates run without a pre-registered test. The disability piece that passes its test models who reports a work-limiting disability, a different measure from who receives disability insurance. Three of the four blind tests compute benefits with our own Python code, and the fourth cuts reported benefits directly. The Axiom rules engine, which encodes the Social Security statute as machine-readable rules, so far reproduces one step of that calculation: a worker's average monthly earnings over the highest-earning years, adjusted for wage growth.

We plan to add earnings, marriage and divorce after 2010 to the projections, apply the retirement earnings test and the family maximum, let claim ages respond to reforms where the data support it, run the full benefit rules in Axiom, and compare the model with public tables from SSA's actuaries, MINT, the Penn Wharton Budget Model and CBO (@sec-remaining). We have compared the PSID's earnings for 1998 to 2004 with a public file of Social Security earnings records, and we plan to compare the model's earnings and whole careers with that file next (@sec-psid).

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Some questions about Social Security need more than a snapshot of one year: who a benefit cut reaches decades from now, or how a higher retirement age plays out across cohorts. Dynamic microsimulation answers them by aging a population of individual people year by year, drawing their earnings, marriages, disabilities, deaths and claims, and applying the program's rules to each life. The Urban Institute's DYNASIM, the Social Security Administration's MINT and the Congressional Budget Office's long-term model, CBOLT, do this for Social Security. Outside analysts can read the results these models publish, but CBO does not publish CBOLT's code, and we found no public code for DYNASIM or MINT with which outsiders could rerun them or reproduce their results [@favreault2015; @smith2021mint8; @cbo2018].

Anyone can read, rerun and check Microcosm Dynamics. It extends Microcosm, PolicyEngine's open cross-sectional microdata for the United States, with a longitudinal layer we estimate on the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID). We publish its code, estimates and tests under the MIT license at `github.com/PolicyEngine/microcosm-dynamics`. The model produces no cost estimates. Its first-estimates report sums weighted benefits and payroll contributions over the projected sample, labels them frame-relative and states that it does not estimate national dollars (`runs/first_estimates_v1.json`). The model computes no actuarial balance and no trust fund depletion date.

The model's generated and forward earnings, its family formation models and its work-limitation disability module each pass a gate: a test on held-out or external data that we register publicly before we run it. We admit a component that faces a gate to the model only after it passes. We take the term from software engineering, where code must clear quality gates before it ships, and from the go/no-go decisions of clinical trials. Before a gate's scored run, we fix the statistics it scores, which we call cells, and a tolerance for each cell. We change them only by a public amendment, which must precede the next scored run. The processes we estimate on the PSID also pass a transport gate, which tests them once we carry them onto the Current Population Survey (CPS) frame, the representative population the model can start from. Four gates pass only under such amendments, which we adopted after an earlier attempt failed (@sec-scoring). They cover the earnings histories the model generates, family formation, the CPS transport and the whole engine, which we fit on data through 2014 and score on its 2015–2019 projections against the PSID. Mortality, claiming, disability-insurance entitlement and the immigrants who enter the population on a schedule run without a gate, and no gate certifies how mortality rates drift over time.

Four blind tests compare the model with results published from DYNASIM3, and none of them uses a gated component. In each test, we post the plan publicly before the run, and two independent readings of DYNASIM3's published values stay sealed until we have committed the model's output to the repository. Each plan, which we call a registration, discloses its participants' exposures, including any to those published values, and a test is blind only as far as those disclosures show. For a one-point cut to cost-of-living adjustments, the model's 2030 benefit changes land within 0.74 percentage points of DYNASIM3's in every age group, and the absolute gap averages 0.38 points. Once we fix the year from which each benefit's cost-of-living increases run, that cut acts mechanically on benefits in payment, which makes this comparison a weak test of behavioral dynamics. When the reduced increases start at each beneficiary's own entitlement year, the absolute gap averages 1.47 points.

Each of the other three tests finds a gap between the two models. Raising the full retirement age to 68 cuts average benefits for people aged 65 to 69 in 2030 by 5.7 percent in the model and 9.9 percent in DYNASIM3, so the model's cut is 4.2 points shallower. A 13 percent benefit cut raises adjusted poverty at age 67 in the 1936–45 birth cohort by 0.46 percentage points in the model and 2 points in DYNASIM3. The model observes only the cohort's odd birth years. DYNASIM3 projects that the headline version of a minimum benefit reaches 6.3 percent of beneficiaries aged 62 and older, and the model finds 7.75 percent. In the model's primary specification, each of the four versions we test reaches more women and fewer men than DYNASIM3 projects. Three of the six alternative specifications put more men, or fewer women, on the minimum than DYNASIM3 does in at least one version. These last two tests apply each reform to incomes the PSID already recorded, while DYNASIM3's figures come from projections its authors published in 2004 and 2006, so a gap in either test can reflect the population's vintage as well as the two models' rules.

The two projection tests, which cover the cost-of-living cut and the higher retirement age, draw no earnings after 2010, count every later year as zero in the benefit formula and check no insured status. The model's forward earnings law, which draws each person's employment and earnings rank every two years, passes its own gate against the PSID's 2016 and 2018 earnings, waves we had in view when we chose the law's structure. We fit that law on PSID earnings through 2014 for ages 25 to 64. It has no fitted distribution above 64 and draws anyone older from its oldest age band. Both projection tests start in 2010 and need earnings for people in their sixties, the ages at which the retirement earnings test withholds benefits from beneficiaries who work before full retirement age. The model computes the projection tests' benefits with Python rules. The Axiom rules engine so far reproduces one piece of those rules, average indexed monthly earnings computed with statutory computation years, while the projection tests count a fixed 35 years. We plan to connect the forward law to the projection tests, apply the retirement earnings test, add behavioral claiming and run the full benefit rules in Axiom (@sec-remaining).

# The model {#sec-model}

The model fits most transitions of individual lives on the PSID, draws claim ages from the Social Security Administration's published awards, and runs these transitions forward, one year at a time, on a population of people. It has three layers. A starting population supplies the people, the projection engine moves each person through one year (`engine/loop.py`), and the rules layer turns the simulated lives into Social Security benefits (`ss/`).

## The starting population

The model is built to start from either Microcosm's certified, representative frame of the United States or a closed PSID cohort; so far, only gate w1 places its processes on the frame, and every projection starts from a PSID cohort. We build the frame from the Current Population Survey (CPS), and it holds 166,302 people in 57,240 households, with a 2024 reference period (`gates.yaml`, gate_w1). We estimate the transitions on the PSID, a multi-decade family panel, and carry them onto the CPS frame. Gate w1, the transport gate, tests whether those transitions reproduce the frame's cross-sectional joint distributions of earnings, age, sex, marital status and household composition.

All four blind tests against DYNASIM3 use a closed PSID cohort (`cohorts/`). We build each comparison's cohort with code that reads the PSID files, and we verify the variable labels that code uses. The two projection tests, which run the engine forward, start from 11,405 members of the 2011 PSID wave. Their earnings histories run from 1968 through 2010, with PSID-reported earnings where the panel has them and imputed or zero values where it does not (@sec-psid).

## The projection engine

Each simulated year, the engine takes every person's record through eight steps in a fixed order (`engine/loop.py`): mortality, aging, the marital core (which updates marital state), fertility, disability, earnings, claiming and household composition. We build each step as a separate component that does its own calculations. The loop fixes only the order of the steps and the flow of marital state: fertility (step 4) and household composition (step 8) both read the one result the marital core (step 3) produces, so every downstream step works from the same marriage history. Scheduled immigrant cohorts enter through a dedicated entry point in the loop, and births come from the fertility step.

The engine takes every random number from a dedicated stream, keyed by draw, period and module, and by person where a step needs it (`engine/rng.py`). The same seed produces an identical projection.

We fit the engine's estimated components only on data dated no later than a boundary year, now 2014 (`engine/refit.py`). We use the boundary to score the engine out of sample. After fitting the whole engine on data through 2014, we project across the later PSID waves and compare the projection with what the PSID recorded. Gate m6 scores that comparison over 2015–2019 (`gates.yaml`, gate_m6). The model treats 2020–2022 as an exogenous shock outside its scope; we publish that window as a diagnostic and keep it out of every gated cell. We hold the fitted parameters, but not every design choice, to data through 2014. We selected gate m6's scored cells with the post-2014 waves in view (`gates.yaml`, gate_m6).

The engine separates scored holdout runs from open forward projections (`engine/support.py`). A scored holdout run may condition on which people the PSID observed in later waves. An open forward projection, which no gate scores, gets no later-wave information: the engine refuses to supply it.

## The rules layer

The rules layer computes Social Security benefits from the engine's output. Its Python oracle, the reference code in `ss/` against which we check the Axiom rules engine, computes average indexed monthly earnings (AIME), the primary insurance amount (PIA), claiming-age adjustments, and spouse and survivor benefits under 42 U.S.C. 415 and 402. It takes its parameters from the PolicyEngine-US parameter tree. The oracle counts computation years in one of two ways (`ss/statutory_aime.py`): a fixed 35 for every worker, or the statutory number, which falls short of 35 for workers who reach 62 with fewer elapsed years.

Axiom, a rules engine that encodes the statute as machine-readable rules, reproduces the oracle's AIME for all 7,486 people we test, using statutory computation years. Those people are the members of the 2011-wave cohort who reach 62 between 1979 and 2030. A bridge program (`axiom_benefit_bridge.py`) passes the cohort's stored earnings histories into the real Axiom engine. With a fixed count of 35 years instead, the oracle's AIME differs from the statutory AIME for 251 of the 7,486, all born before 1929.

We compare Axiom with the oracle on AIME alone, and both compute it on an old-age basis that assumes no period of disability. We give Axiom and the oracle the same input definitions, and the match depends on them. Both treat PSID labor income as covered earnings, and both receive the same zero or imputed values for years before 1968, years after 2010 and years absent from the panel. Of the 320,375 earnings rows the bridge sends, 194,465 hold zeros or imputed values. Axiom and the oracle produce identical output from identical records. The match says nothing about whether either AIME equals a person's true AIME. Axiom's Social Security encodings await acceptance, so the blind tests that compute benefits run on the Python oracle (`cola_track_a/benefits.py`).

# What the model covers today {#sec-coverage}

None of the four blind tests uses a component that passes a gate (@tbl-coverage). Of the four blind tests, exercise 1 projects how a one-point cut to cost-of-living adjustments changes benefits in 2030, and exercise 3 does the same for a full retirement age of 68. These two are the projection tests. The other two apply a reform to incomes the PSID recorded: a uniform 13 percent benefit cut in exercise 2 and a minimum benefit in exercise 4. Each verdict we report comes from its gate's committed result file under `runs/`. Gates 1, 2, w1 and m6 pass only under public amendments, which we adopted after earlier attempts failed (@sec-scoring).

| Component | What the model does | Test and status | Used in the blind tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recorded earnings | PSID head and spouse labor income, 1968–2022, with odd years after 1996 filled from neighboring years (exercise 4 reads the PSID's off-year reports for 2001–2021) and other missing years set to zero | Data, with imputed gaps | Yes, in exercises 1, 3 and 4 |
| Generated earnings histories | A backcast process that generates earnings careers | gate 1: passes against held-out panel moments (`runs/gate1_rank_knn_v5.json`) | No |
| Forward earnings | Rank-chain law fitted on 2014 and earlier, ages 25–64 | gate m6: passes, 4 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate_m6_candidate3_v1.json`) | No |
| Earnings test | SSA's exempt amounts for 2000–2026 and the statutory formula that projects later years | Tested against SSA's published amounts; not applied | No |
| Mortality | Death probabilities by age band and sex | Not gated; gate m6 certifies nothing about mortality drift | Exercises 1 and 3 use SSA's 2004 period life table; exercise 2 annuitizes wealth with NCHS 2000 tables |
| Disability | Work-limitation incidence, recovery, occupancy and exits near full retirement age | gate m4: passes, 5 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate_m4_hazard_v1.json`) | No |
| SSDI entitlement | Awards, recoveries and conversion at full retirement age, at rates through 2008 | Not gated | Yes, in exercises 1 and 3 |
| Claiming | SSA's claim-age distribution of retired-worker awards (Annual Statistical Supplement, Table 6.B5.1), by sex and entitlement year | Not gated | Yes, in exercises 1 and 3, with no response to reform |
| Marriage and fertility | Marriage, divorce, remarriage, widowhood and births | gate 2: passes, 4 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate2_hazard_v16.json`) | No |
| Household composition | Who lives with whom | gate 2b: passes, 4 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate2b_hazard_v9.json`) | No |
| Marriage by earnings | The joint of marital status and earnings | gate 2c: passes, 4 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate2c_hazard_v2.json`) | No |
| Entrants | Scheduled immigrant cohorts; births come from the fertility step | Report-only; not gated | No |
| Base frame | Transport of PSID processes onto the CPS frame | gate w1: passes (`runs/gate_w1_candidate4_v1.json`) | No |
| Benefit rules | AIME, PIA, auxiliaries in the Python oracle | Reference implementation | Yes, in exercises 1, 3 and 4 |
| Axiom execution | Statutory rules in the Axiom engine | AIME matches the oracle for 7,486 of 7,486 people | No |
| SSI, income and poverty | Static SSI response and an adjusted poverty measure | Registered test, exercise 2 | Yes, in exercise 2, which cuts reported benefits directly |
| Wealth and pensions | PSID wealth annuitized into income | No projection | Exercise 2 only |

: What each component of the model does, its test and status, and which of the four blind tests against DYNASIM3 use it. SSDI is Social Security Disability Insurance; SSI is Supplemental Security Income. {#tbl-coverage}

**Earnings.** The model has three kinds of earnings (recorded, generated and projected), and the blind tests use only the recorded kind. Recorded earnings are the labor income of PSID heads and spouses for income years 1968–2022 (`data/family.py`). The PSID asks about them every year through 1996. After that it interviews every other year, and each interview centers on the year before it. The model's main earnings panel reads only those years, so we fill the odd years from neighboring years and set other years without a usable record to zero (@sec-psid). For the 7,486 members of the 2011-wave cohort who reach 62 between 1979 and 2030, 128,033 of their 253,943 career years through 2010, about half, hold values we imputed or filled with zero. The oracle computes benefits directly from these recorded careers. The projection tests use careers through 2010. The minimum-benefit test, exercise 4, reads a longer span of the same panel. For the odd-numbered years from 2001 to 2021, it reads the labor income each following wave reports for the year before last.

Generated earnings come from a backcast, a backward-looking process that produces earnings careers. Gate 1 scores that process against held-out panel moments, relative to the panel's own noise floor, and it passes (`runs/gate1_rank_knn_v5.json`).

Projected earnings come from the forward earnings law (`engine/forward_earnings.py`), a rank chain we fit on earnings the PSID observed through 2014 at ages 25 to 64. Every two years, the law draws whether each person works and where they rank in the earnings distribution, then converts that rank to dollars with the national average wage index, which the law projects from a log-linear trend it fits on 2005–2014. It has no fitted distribution above 64 and draws people over 64 from its oldest age band. The engine assigns fixed zero earnings to anyone without a fitted 2014 earnings state (`engine/earnings_domain.py`).

The forward law passes gate m6 in 4 of 5 random seeds, its only certification (`runs/gate_m6_candidate3_v1.json`; @sec-scoring). Gate m6 scores the whole engine's holdout projection (@sec-model), and its earnings cells compare persistence, growth, mobility, low earnings and the zero-earnings rate in 2016 and 2018 with the PSID's records. In all five seeds, the projection's two-year growth in log earnings at ages 25 to 44 runs 2.7 to 5.2 log points lower than the PSID's, and its 10th percentile of positive earnings at those ages runs 15 to 24 percent lower. The correlation of log earnings four years apart runs 0.74 to 0.76 in the projection and 0.67 to 0.71 in the PSID. We fit the law's parameters only on data through 2014, but we selected its structure with the later waves in view (`gates.yaml`, gate_m6).

No blind test yet draws forward earnings, and the projection tests draw no earnings after 2010 (`cola_track_a/adapters.py`). Their projections begin in 2010, four years before the forward law's 2014 fit boundary, and they reach ages above 64, where the law has no fitted distribution. The retirement earnings test withholds benefits from beneficiaries in their sixties who work before full retirement age. Both projection tests' specifications list it among the differences from DYNASIM3 that they leave out, and no projection applies it yet. The model already holds the earnings test's parameters: SSA's exempt amounts for 2000–2026, which we checked against SSA's published history, and the statutory formula that projects later years.

**Family.** Three family gates pass, each in 4 of 5 seeds. Gate 2 scores marriage, divorce, remarriage, widowhood, the stock in each marital state and births (`runs/gate2_hazard_v16.json`). Gate 2b scores household composition (`runs/gate2b_hazard_v9.json`), and gate 2c scores the joint distribution of marital status and earnings (`runs/gate2c_hazard_v2.json`). The projection tests use none of these gated family models. Their marital step sets a person's status to widowed when a linked spouse dies in the simulation, and it draws no marriages and no divorces.

**Disability, mortality and claiming.** The disability module passes gate m4 in 5 of 5 seeds (`runs/gate_m4_hazard_v1.json`). It models self-reported work limitation: incidence, recovery, occupancy and exits near full retirement age. Gate m4 scores it against held-out PSID employment-status records and against the age shape and exit composition of SSA's 2023 disability-insurance statistics. It never scores SSA's levels. Work limitation is a different concept from a Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) award. The projection tests use a separate SSDI entitlement component, which draws awards, recoveries and conversion at full retirement age at rates observed through 2008 (`engine/di_entitlement.py`). No gate scores it.

The engine's mortality step uses a table of death probabilities by age band and sex, and gate m6 certifies nothing about how mortality drifts over time. The projection tests use SSA's 2004 period life table. Each year we multiply its death probabilities by the ratio of that year's age-sex-adjusted death rate to the 2004 rate, both from the 2008 Trustees Report's intermediate assumptions. We use one ratio for ages under 65 and another for 65 and over, and each applies to men and women alike. The 2008 Trustees Report prints no projected death probabilities by single year of age and sex. SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary publishes such probabilities in downloadable files alongside its Reports, which we found for the 2014 Report onward; for the 2026 Report, the men's intermediate file is <https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/Downloadables/CY/DeathProbsE_M_Alt2_TR2026.csv>. Claiming runs with no gate. The claiming step draws a claim age from SSA's published distribution of retired-worker awards by sex and entitlement year (`claiming.py`). For entitlement years after 2008, the projection tests reuse the 2008 distribution. No claim responds to a reform. Exercise 3, which raises the full retirement age to 68, therefore holds each person's projected claim age fixed under the reform. Its registration, the plan we post before the run, lists claiming responses only as alternatives that we report beside the main result (@sec-blind).

**Population.** Gate w1 passes (`runs/gate_w1_candidate4_v1.json`). When we carry the transitions we estimate on the PSID onto the CPS frame (@sec-model), they match the frame on all 44 gated cells: 43 cross-sectional joint distributions and one ordering check. The entrant schedule lets new people enter a projection. We report its output, and no gate scores it. No fitted law takes that output as an input.

**Rules.** Exercises 1, 3 and 4 compute benefits with the Python oracle (`cola_track_a/benefits.py`). The projection tests count a fixed 35 computation years for every worker. Axiom, using the statutory count instead, reproduces the oracle's AIME for all 7,486 cohort members we test (@sec-model). Exercise 2 applies no benefit rules. It cuts reported Social Security income by 13 percent inside an income concept we define in Python, applies a static Supplemental Security Income (SSI) offset and computes an adjusted poverty measure. It also annuitizes PSID wealth into income with NCHS 2000 tables.

# How the model is scored {#sec-scoring}

We admit to the model any component that passes a gate, and four components run in it without one: mortality, claiming, disability-insurance entitlement and entrants. Each gate names its coverage, the held-out data it scores against, the cells it scores and a tolerance for each cell. We write all of a gate's terms into `gates.yaml` and fix them before the scored run. We call each version of the component under test a candidate, and we register it, give it one scored run against its gate and commit the result under `runs/` whatever the verdict. A failed candidate therefore stays in the record next to the one that passed. We change a gate's terms only by public amendment, which must precede the next scored run.

We use four kinds of gate: holdout, anchor, transport and temporal holdout. A holdout gate scores a component on persons we excluded from its fit. Gate 1 holds out 20 percent of persons. The family gates hold out half, split by person for gates 2 and 2b and by couple for gate 2c, so that both members of a couple fall in the same half. Each of these gates scores every candidate on the same five random seeds, and gate 1 scores one classifier test over 20. To judge the model against the sampling variation of the data a gate scores, we set each cell's tolerance against a noise floor: the discrepancy between two disjoint halves we draw from one real panel. A seed passes only if every gated cell stays within its tolerance, and a family gate needs at least four of its five seeds to pass. An anchor gate scores a component on a person-disjoint half of the panel and against external administrative publications. The disability gate compares the age shape and exit composition of work-limitation estimates with SSA's 2023 disability-insurance statistics. It scores none of SSA's levels.

The transport gate, w1, tests whether the processes we estimate on the PSID reproduce the CPS frame's cross-sectional joint distributions. The temporal holdout, m6, fits the whole engine on data from 2014 and earlier and projects it forward. It scores projected marital flows and disability flows for 2015 to 2019, and earnings moments for 2016 and 2018, against PSID records. It publishes the 2020–2022 window as a diagnostic and scores none of it. Each gate also states what it does not certify. Gate m6 certifies nothing about how mortality and widowhood drift over time, or about entrants.

Four gates pass only under amendments we adopted after an earlier candidate failed: gates 1, 2, w1 and m6. Gate 1 passes under two amendments, and `gates.yaml` records both (`gate_1`). In a distinguishability test, a classifier tries to tell generated careers from recorded ones. The first amendment makes a failing test of this kind report-only, a status for cells we publish with no tolerance, and adds a gated block that scores the careers in benefit space, which weights earnings the way the benefit formula does. The second scores another distinguishability test by its mean over 20 seeds. When we adopted it, a committed diagnostic had already put the failed candidate's 20-seed mean at 0.523, under the gate's threshold of 0.53 (`runs/c10_diagnostics_v1.json`). The passing candidate, `runs/gate1_rank_knn_v5.json`, is identical to its failed predecessor. Gate 2 passes on its 16th candidate, a changed model, under an amendment to the gate's estimator and a split of the gate into parts that we score separately. We adopted both after earlier candidates failed (`gates.yaml`, `gate_2`). The amendment scores the gate by its mean over 20 draws. The split leaves marriage and fertility in gate 2, and we score household composition and marriage by earnings in separate gates, 2b and 2c.

Gate w1 passes under three amendments, each of which we adopted after a candidate failed. Together they make 21 cells report-only, and narrow the one ordering check the gate scores. The third makes four household-size shares report-only: those for one, three, four, and five or more people. Among the gated cross-sectional cells, candidate 3 had failed only those four, and it put the one-person share at 0.19 against the frame's 0.08. We had named those cells as risks in the forecast for the second amendment, before candidate 3 ran, and the third amendment states that candidate 3 would pass its terms. As at gate 1, the passing candidate is identical to its failed predecessor (`runs/NOTES-gate_w1_candidate4.md`).

At gate m6, the third candidate passes under one amendment, which restricts the earnings cells to people who have a fitted 2014 earnings state and re-derives the cells' noise floors. Candidate 1 failed before that amendment and candidate 2 after it (`runs/gate_m6_candidate1_v1.json`, `runs/gate_m6_candidate2_v1.json`; `gates.yaml`, gate_m6, `runs/m6_holdout_floors_v4.json`). The restriction drops 2,722 of the 13,163 people the earnings cells had scored. The re-derived floors raise the tolerance on the 10th percentile of positive earnings at ages 25 to 44 from 0.221 to 0.284, and three of candidate 3's four passing seeds score between those two values. In every seed, candidate 3's remarriage rate runs 27 to 51 percent higher than the PSID's. Other gates pass as well, gate m4 among them.

We run the blind tests against DYNASIM3 (@sec-blind) under the gates' procedure, with no tolerances. Because DYNASIM3 is another published model and not ground truth, each comparison reports its gaps without grading them.

Over the long horizon, assumptions outweigh the model's machinery, so we limit what the model claims according to how far ahead it projects. The 2025 Trustees Report puts the 75-year actuarial balance at −3.82 percent of taxable payroll on intermediate assumptions, −0.33 percent on low-cost assumptions and −8.60 percent on high-cost ones [@ssa2025trustees]. That low-to-high spread, 8.27 percentage points of taxable payroll, exceeds twice the intermediate deficit. We therefore sort the model's outputs into three tiers.

Tier 1 covers distributional reform analysis that holds the population and the assumption path fixed. Baseline and reform share much of the demographic uncertainty, and we expect that shared part to cancel when we difference them. No gate measures how much of it does. The tier design calls for labeling the parts that do not cancel, claiming responses among them, and for anchoring claiming-response ranges to quasi-experimental evidence [@mastrobuoni2009; @behaghelblau2012]. Exercise 3's claiming alternatives rest on no such evidence: they delay claims by the full rise in the retirement age, up to age 70, for projected claimants at 65 or older in one and for every projected claimant in the other. Tier 2 covers near-term outputs: covered earnings, beneficiary counts, claiming ages, average benefits and disability incidence. Because administrative publications report all five every year, we can score each against those publications annually. `gates.yaml` names gate 3 for this tier but gives it no cells or tolerances, and gate 3 has never run. Tier 3 covers the long horizon. For it, the design calls for sensitivity surfaces over documented assumption ranges, computed on named assumption paths, among them the Trustees' intermediate path, and presents none of them as the model's own forecast.

# Four blind tests against DYNASIM3 {#sec-blind}

Four blind tests set the model's results against DYNASIM3's published values. Two project benefit reforms to 2030: exercise 1 cuts each cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) by one percentage point, and exercise 3 raises the full retirement age to 68 [@urban2010detailsmatter]. Two calculate directly on incomes the PSID observed: exercise 2 cuts every benefit by 13 percent [@butrica2004boomers], and exercise 4 adds a minimum benefit [@favreault2006minimum]. The COLA test lands within 0.74 percentage points of DYNASIM3 in every age group. Each of the other three finds a place where the two models differ.

An interactive scorecard at <https://microcosm.institute/dynamics/scorecard> publishes every cell, each test's timeline and every registered alternative, a variant that a test's registration names before the run and that we report beside the test's main result. We post every registration and every result as a public comment on issue #42 of the repository, <https://github.com/PolicyEngine/microcosm-dynamics/issues/42>.

## The protocol

In each test, a separate comparison workstream, working apart from the model's builders, makes two independent readings of DYNASIM3's published values, transcribing them from tables or digitizing them from figures. It reconciles the two readings and seals the files under SHA-256 hashes, digital fingerprints that change if a file changes. We ratify the model specification and freeze it at a named commit, a fixed version of the code in the repository. A forecaster blind to the sealed values then predicts both the model's result and its gap as intervals, and we hash the forecast. The registration carries the specification hash, the commit, the primary row that the test reports as its result, the registered alternatives we report beside it, and the forecast. No registered alternative may replace the primary row after the fact. The model runs and writes its output to a file, the artifact, and we score only that output. We check the artifact and commit it, and only then does the comparison lane open the seal. We publish the comparison whatever the outcome. No test has an acceptance threshold.

The hashes show that neither the sealed DYNASIM3 files nor the artifact files changed. Commit times and the recorded step order show that we committed each output before its test's seal opened. Neither can show whether a participant ever saw a DYNASIM3 value. Each registration discloses its participants' exposures, and a test is blind only as far as those disclosures show. The four tests ran on 23, 25 and 27 September 2026, in the order 1, 3, 2, 4.

The AI model that coordinated the build, Claude Opus 5.5, saw the digitized exercise 1 values on 22 September, in a report that may also have held the exercise 3 bars. It later wrote builder and reviewer briefs, and registration 13 states that none contains a comparator value or a choice informed by one. On 24 September, the exercise 3 comparison lane found five copies of restricted material from the 2010 report where builders could reach them. The same day, a scratchpad folder the builder agents shared held files whose names suggest Figure 2 material, exercise 1's comparator reconciliation files, two PDFs the size of the 2004 and 2006 reports, and extracts of restricted pages of the 2004 report. No builder report cites these files, and the registrations cannot rule out that builders opened them. The author of the exercise 2 plan read a page of the 2004 report that includes results prose, and the author of the first exercise 4 plan read one withheld sentence, which describes a table of expenditure paths outside exercise 4's targets.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. COLA cut | 2026-09-23 23:06:06 | 23:06–23:31 | 23:40:38 | 23:42:53 |
| 3. Full retirement age 68 | 2026-09-25 22:35:30 | 22:36–23:07 | 23:27:01 | 23:40:59 |
| 2. 13 percent cut | 2026-09-27 05:01:06 | 05:01:49–05:03:29 | 05:06:13 | 05:29:39 |
| 4. Minimum benefit | 2026-09-27 12:18:29 | 12:19:17–12:19:48 | 12:36:32 | 12:58:12 |

## The projections

Both projection tests run the same engine configuration. The engine seeds a closed cohort from the PSID's 2011 wave and ages it to 2030 in 20 random draws, with 2008-vintage mortality and disability rates. We take COLAs for 2008–2030 and the average wage index for 1975–2030 from the 2008 Trustees Report's intermediate assumptions. Those assumptions put the COLAs for 2008, 2009 and 2010 at 2.7, 2.5 and 2.8 percent, where SSA's realized COLAs were 5.8, 0 and 0 percent. The Python oracle computes benefits with a fixed 35 computation years for every worker. The projections draw no earnings after 2010, so the oracle computes each worker's AIME from earnings for 1968 through 2010 and counts every year before 1968 or after 2010 as zero. Neither projection checks insured status, so any projected claimant whose career through 2010 gives a positive AIME becomes a retired-worker beneficiary, however few years that career covers. For people already retired when the projection starts, the oracle takes their observed 2010 benefit amounts, and for disabled workers it uses approximate benefit levels.

Each test reports the percent change in mean Social Security benefits in 2030 for five groups by age in 2030: 50–61, 62–64, 65–69, 70–79 and 80 and older. We compute the change as a weighted ratio of the reform and baseline means. We measure the model's uncertainty two ways. The draw standard deviation captures the variation across the 20 projections. For the half-sample floor, we split the sample into two halves that share no person and no family unit, take the mean absolute difference between them, and average it over five random splits. The floor shows how far the estimate moves from sampling alone. Under normality, the expected floor is about 1.6 times the full-sample standard error. The draw standard deviation reaches 0.36 points in exercise 1's primary row, at ages 50–61, and 0.24 points in exercise 3, at ages 62–64, where the floor is 0.09. The comparison lane digitizes DYNASIM3's projection values from a figure, so each value carries a digitization interval and no standard error.

### Exercise 1: a one-point COLA cut

Exercise 1 reduces each annual COLA by one percentage point, starting in 2010. DYNASIM3's values come from Figure 2 of *Details Matter*, which reports DYNASIM3 run 614 on the 2008 Trustees assumptions [@urban2010detailsmatter].

| Age in 2030 | Microcosm Dynamics | DYNASIM3 | Gap (pp) | Half-sample floor |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50–61 | −7.77 | −7.15 | −0.62 | 0.27 |
| 62–64 | −3.64 | −3.79 | +0.14 | 0.34 |
| 65–69 | −6.26 | −6.36 | +0.10 | 0.12 |
| 70–79 | −12.22 | −11.94 | −0.28 | 0.16 |
| 80+ | −17.92 | −18.66 | +0.74 | 0.09 |

: Exercise 1, a one-point COLA cut: percent change in average benefits in 2030, by age in 2030. {#tbl-ex1}

Every age group lands within 0.74 percentage points of DYNASIM3, and the mean absolute gap comes to 0.38 points. The two models order all five groups the same way. The gaps at 62–64 and 65–69 are smaller than the half-sample floor, while those at 50–61, 70–79 and 80 and older exceed it.

The largest gap, 0.74 points, sits in the oldest group. The model's timing convention applies 21 reduced increases by 2030, so nobody aged 80 or older loses more than 18.56 percent. DYNASIM3's −18.66 percent sits 0.10 points past that bound, close to the figure's reading resolution of about 0.09 points. A registered alternative that counts the December 2030 increase brings the oldest group within 0.06 points. It also makes every other group's cut 0.8 to 1.5 points deeper than DYNASIM3's. No single registered timing convention fits all five groups. Two untested hypotheses could explain the oldest group's gap: the two models may time COLAs differently for the oldest cohorts, or they may hold different mixes of survivors, including survivors whose cost-of-living increases run from an earlier year. The published figure cannot tell them apart.

The 50–61 group consists almost entirely of disabled workers, and the model's cut there runs 0.62 points deeper. Two untested hypotheses could account for it: how long the disabled workers on the rolls at the projection's start have already received benefits, and the 2008-vintage award and termination rates.

Exercise 1 is a weak test of behavioral dynamics: once we fix the year from which each benefit's cost-of-living increases run, the reform acts mechanically on benefits in payment. The registration lists six alternatives, each changing one convention. An alternative that starts the reduced increases at each beneficiary's own entitlement year widens the mean gap to 1.47 points, and one built on the 2009 PSID wave gives a mean gap of 0.37.

### Exercise 3: a full retirement age of 68

Exercise 3 raises the full retirement age gradually from 2010 until it reaches 68 for people turning 62 in 2022 or later. DYNASIM3's values come from the "Increase FRA to 68" bars in the same figure [@urban2010detailsmatter]. The test applies the reform to each of exercise 1's 20 projected paths and holds claiming ages fixed at their baseline values.

| Age in 2030 | Microcosm Dynamics | DYNASIM3 | Gap (pp) | Half-sample floor |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50–61 | 0.00 | 0.00 (reading) | 0.00 | 0.00 |
| 62–64 | −4.73 | −5.12 | +0.39 | 0.09 |
| 65–69 | −5.68 | −9.90 | +4.22 | 0.11 |
| 70–79 | −5.24 | −4.15 | −1.09 | 0.07 |
| 80+ | −0.75 | −0.60 | −0.14 | 0.11 |

: Exercise 3, a full retirement age of 68: percent change in average benefits in 2030, by age in 2030. {#tbl-ex3}

At 65–69, DYNASIM3's cut is 1.74 times the model's, a gap of 4.22 points. That one group carries 72 percent of the mean absolute gap of 1.17 points. Nine of the ten pairwise orderings agree. DYNASIM3's 50–61 bar shows no visible height, so its zero is a digitizer's reading, and the drawing's resolution of about 0.09 points bounds that reading. The model's estimate is consistent with zero at that resolution.

The 65–69 group covers the 1961–1965 birth cohorts, whose full retirement age rises by 12 months. At fixed claim ages, that rise cuts a retired worker's benefit by 6.25 to 7.69 percent and a spouse's excess by at most 10 percent, and it leaves a disabled worker's benefit where it was. To reach DYNASIM3's 9.90 percent through those factors, the group would have to consist almost entirely of spouses' excesses starting at 65. In the model, disabled and converted-disabled benefits make up 17.8 percent of the group's baseline dollars. DYNASIM3's 65–69 bar therefore includes more than the age-factor cut at fixed claim ages.

Three untested hypotheses could supply the rest. DYNASIM3's 2004 primer, which predates run 614, says its benefit calculator checks insured status and applies the retirement earnings test [@favreault2004dynasim3]. The primer also says that DYNASIM3's claiming hazards include Social Security policy parameters, with separate equations by the ratio of recent earnings to the earnings test's exempt amount, and it aligns employment at ages 65 to 69 to Trustees targets. Exercise 3's projection does none of these. The first hypothesis is a retirement earnings test extended to 68, which would withhold benefits from people still working. The model pays gross benefits, applies no earnings test and draws no earnings after 2010, so testing this hypothesis requires forward earnings. The second is a claiming response that shifts claims later. The third is an average over all living people in place of recipients alone, which counts a postponed claimant as zero. A diagnostic that applies that averaging to the model's own claiming alternative moves the 65–69 change to −8.68 percent.

The registration lists eight alternatives, which vary the PSID wave, the phase-in schedule, survivor rules, a claiming response, benefit types and the statistic. None comes within 3.9 points of DYNASIM3 at 65–69.

Exercise 3's first registration, number 14 on issue #42, stopped before scoring. The test runner's membership guard, which then halted any run in which the baseline and the reform counted different people as beneficiaries, ended it. By then the run had computed the primary row in memory. It had printed and recorded no value, no artifact existed, and the seal stayed closed. Registration 15 carried the same forecast and produced the scored run, after a reviewed change that makes the guard halt only on membership differences it does not explain.

## The static calculations

Exercises 2 and 4 apply each reform to incomes the PSID observed and count who it affects. They project nothing and model no behavioral response. The model's figures describe realized incomes, while DYNASIM3's come from projections its authors published in 2004 for exercise 2 and in 2006 for exercise 4 [@butrica2004boomers; @favreault2006minimum]. A gap in either test can reflect the population's vintage as well as the two models' rules.

### Exercise 2: a uniform 13 percent benefit cut

Exercise 2 cuts every Social Security benefit by 13 percent from 2004. DYNASIM3's values come from Tables 19 and 21 of Butrica and Uccello's *How Will Boomers Fare at Retirement?*, which report what the authors call adjusted poverty at age 67 for the 1936–45 birth cohort, with and without the cut [@butrica2004boomers]. The test reports the change in the poverty rate in percentage points. The model's sample holds 483 people whom the PSID observes at exactly age 67, born in 1937, 1939, 1941, 1943 and 1945. We attach each person to their family's income and poverty threshold. The report prints poverty levels as whole percentages, so each printed change carries an open rounding interval of ±1 percentage point.

| Group | n | Microcosm Dynamics | DYNASIM3 | Gap (pp) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All | 483 | +0.46 | +2 | −1.54 |
| Women | 249 | +0.35 | +3 | −2.65 |
| Men | 234 | +0.60 | +1 | −0.40 |
| Married | 331 | +0.60 | +1 | −0.40 |
| Widowed | 44 | +0.45 | +2 | −1.55 |
| Divorced | 60 | 0 | +5 | −5.00 |
| Never married | 14 | 0 | +5 | −5.00 |

: Exercise 2, a uniform 13 percent benefit cut: change in adjusted poverty at age 67, in percentage points. {#tbl-ex2}

The cut raises adjusted poverty by 0.46 percentage points in the model and by 2 points in DYNASIM3. The model's change comes out smaller in all seven groups. Men and married people fall inside DYNASIM3's rounding interval, and the other five groups fall outside it. Before the cut, 25 sample members are poor, and four more cross the poverty line under it. Each average-weight observation moves the headline by 0.21 points. No divorced or never-married member crosses, so both groups change by zero. Without a crosser, we cannot estimate the uncertainty of either group's change, however large the group. The model's poverty levels run lower than DYNASIM3's in six of seven groups before the cut and in all seven after it.

The model's adjusted poverty rate before the cut is 3.1 percent, with a standard error of 0.87 points from the PSID's sampling design. It is 4.1 percent for women, 1.9 for men, 2.2 for married people, 1.7 for widowed, 5.6 for divorced and 14.0 for never-married people. On reported family money income, which keeps reported asset income in place of the wealth annuity, the same sample's poverty rate is 3.8 percent. The headline change has a design standard error of 0.25 points, and the change for women 0.28. The 34 members whose marital status we cannot classify count in the rows for everyone, women and men, and in no marital row.

The registration lists ten alternatives, each changing one input. They vary the birth years covered, the SSI response, the income unit, asset income, employer pension balances, the poverty standard, the life table and the threshold schedule. Five leave every poverty outcome where it was, and none brings the headline inside DYNASIM3's interval. The closest covers all ten birth years and gives +0.62. The untested hypotheses include thinner PSID coverage of low-income unmarried people and whole-family income standing in for an individual's resources. They also include income sources the report does not name and self-reported benefits that may be net of Medicare premiums. A fifth is timing: the model uses incomes realized from 2004 to 2012, while DYNASIM3 projects from the 2002 Trustees assumptions.

### Exercise 4: a minimum benefit

Exercise 4 adds a minimum benefit tied to years of work. Its four versions combine price or wage indexing with a standard or generous schedule, and an across-the-board cut finances each one. They are options 2, 3, 4 and 5, and we take option 2 as the headline. DYNASIM3's values come from Table 6 of Favreault, Mermin and Steuerle's *Minimum Benefits in Social Security*, which reports the 2025 shares of beneficiaries aged 62 and older who receive the minimum, for everyone, men and women [@favreault2006minimum]. The model's sample holds 2,135 Social Security recipients in the PSID's 2023 wave, with incomes for 2022. The report's options take effect in 2007. We move every policy date back three years, to 2004, so that the 2022 snapshot covers 19 entitlement years, 2004 to 2022, as DYNASIM3's 2025 figures cover 2007 to 2025. A registered alternative that keeps the report's 2007 dates puts the headline share at 6.83 percent. We count a person when their benefit rests on the minimum, through their own record or through a linked spouse's or survivor's benefit.

| 2 (headline) | All | 7.75 | 6.3 | +1.45 |
| 2 | Men | 2.36 | 4.8 | −2.44 |
| 2 | Women | 11.67 | 7.6 | +4.07 |
| 3 | All | 11.12 | 11.3 | −0.18 |
| 3 | Men | 3.23 | 8.7 | −5.47 |
| 3 | Women | 16.86 | 13.4 | +3.46 |
| 4 | All | 24.56 | 18.7 | +5.86 |
| 4 | Men | 13.42 | 14.4 | −0.98 |
| 4 | Women | 32.66 | 22.0 | +10.66 |
| 5 | All | 31.47 | 29.3 | +2.17 |
