| 5 | Women | 40.36 | 33.2 | +7.16 |

: Exercise 4, a minimum benefit: percent of beneficiaries aged 62 and older who receive the minimum. {#tbl-ex4}

In every option of the primary row, the model's share runs lower than DYNASIM3's for men and higher for women. The rows for everyone mask the split by sex: under option 3 the model lands 0.18 points from DYNASIM3 for everyone, yet 5.47 points under it for men and 3.46 points over it for women. Both models rank the four options the same way, and both give women a higher share than men in every option. The mean absolute gap across the 12 cells comes to 4.09 points. The untested hypotheses include the difference between a realized 2022 population and a 2025 projection, the source of each person's PIA, the completeness of PSID earnings histories, and records whose benefits began as disability benefits. They also include 60 auxiliary beneficiaries whom the model cannot link to any worker.

In the primary row, we build each person's PIA from the earnings history. A registered alternative that takes the PIA from the benefit the person receives lowers the mean gap to 1.60 points, and under options 2 and 4 it puts more men on the minimum than DYNASIM3 does, at 7.30 and 14.96 percent against 4.8 and 14.4. For the 1,799 records with both measures, the PIA implied by the benefit is 1.11 times the one built from the earnings history at the median and 2.89 times at the 90th percentile. Two more alternatives break the split by sex. One that applies the across-the-board cut after the minimum gives women a lower share than DYNASIM3's under options 2, 3 and 5, and one that uses a 35-year divisor for disability-origin PIAs gives men a higher share than DYNASIM3's under option 4. No alternative can replace the primary row, whose mean gap of 4.09 points remains the test's result.

## What the four tests show and what they cannot

Under the COLA cut, the model lands within 0.74 points of DYNASIM3 in every age group. In the full-retirement-age test, the two models differ by 4.22 points in one age group, 65–69. The model's poverty response to the 13 percent cut comes out smaller in every group, and in every option of the primary row the model puts a smaller share of men and a larger share of women on the minimum benefit than DYNASIM3 does. Three of the six registered alternatives break that split in at least one option. We score the blind forecasts separately from the comparisons. The forecast intervals contain every projection estimate, and in each projection test one gap falls outside its interval. In the static tests, the forecast intervals exclude the model's own values more often than DYNASIM3's.

Each gap measures a disagreement between two models. No test covers DYNASIM4, the current generation of DYNASIM. The tests establish parity with neither DYNASIM3 nor DYNASIM4, and they do not certify the model. Exercises 1, 3 and 4 compute benefits with Python rules, and exercise 2 cuts reported benefits directly. None of the four runs these rules in the Axiom rules engine. We plan to run the full benefit rules in Axiom as separate work (@sec-remaining). The static tests set observed incomes against DYNASIM3's projections and never touch the projection engine, while the projection tests exercise that engine without forward earnings, a retirement earnings test or behavioral claiming. Because neither the COLA cut nor the higher retirement age is current law, no observed outcome can check either model.

The registered alternatives measure how sensitive the model is to its own conventions and reveal nothing about how DYNASIM3 computes its results. Each explanation we offer for the gaps stays a hypothesis until a registered test addresses it.

# The PSID's limits {#sec-psid}

The PSID supplies the model's careers, family events and disability transitions, and its design limits what the model can learn from it. Social Security's benefit formula averages a worker's highest 35 years of indexed earnings, so the model needs earnings across whole careers. The PSID has interviewed the same families and their descendants since 1968, every year through 1997 and every other year since, and anyone can obtain its data [@mcgonagle2012psid]. MINT and CBOLT run on SSA's administrative earnings records (@sec-related), and SSA has a legal obligation to protect the confidentiality of the people in its records [@compson2011epuf]. The PSID is small, it follows a population defined in 1968, it has lost many of its original members, its documented earnings problems concentrate among low earners, and the careers the model builds from it have gaps (@tbl-psid-limits).

**Size.** The PSID began in 1968 with 4,802 families holding 18,230 people, and in 2023 it interviewed 9,152 families holding 24,536 people [@psid2025usermanual]. The Current Population Survey's Annual Social and Economic Supplement, the main source of Microcosm's frame, draws a sample of about 95,000 households each year [@census2024asectechdoc]. Moffitt and Zhang count the PSID's sample size as a weakness, because it "often does not permit much subgroup analysis or distributional analyses" [@moffitt2018volatility]. Exercise 2 shows the constraint. Its sample holds 483 people whom the PSID observes at exactly age 67, so each average-weight observation moves its headline by 0.21 percentage points. None of its 14 never-married members crosses the poverty line under the cut (@sec-blind).

**Selection.** The 1968 sample joined a nationally representative sample of 2,930 families from the University of Michigan's Survey Research Center (SRC) with an oversample of 1,872 low-income families from the Census Bureau's Survey of Economic Opportunity (SEO) [@psid2025usermanual]. Of the families selected in 1968, 76 percent gave an interview [@fitzgerald1998attrition]. The PSID follows everyone who lived in those families and anyone later born to or adopted by them, including when they form new families. People who marry into the sample stay in it only while they live with a sample member [@psid2025usermanual]. The original design did not represent families who arrived after 1968, and it records post-1968 immigrants only while they live with a sample member [@psid2025usermanual]. The PSID later added two immigrant refresher samples: 511 families in 1997 and 1999, too few to analyze immigrant subgroups, and a 2017 sample with 455 completed interviews [@mcgonagle2012psid; @johnson2018fifty]. In 1997 the PSID cut its core sample from about 8,500 families to about 6,300, mostly from the low-income oversample [@psid2025usermanual]. The PSID publishes weights for these unequal chances of selection. It calibrates its cross-sectional weights to population characteristics from the CPS or the American Community Survey for the year in question, and it does not calibrate its longitudinal weights to outside population estimates each wave [@chang2023xsweights2021].

The model keeps the low-income oversample and both immigrant refreshers. Shin and Solon leave the oversample out of their estimates because of irregularities in its selection: by the account of a 1996 memo they cite, the firm that chose its low-income households sent the PSID only 55 percent of eligible nonwhite households and 21 percent of eligible white ones [@shin2008trends]. Dynan, Elmendorf and Sichel leave it out for the same reason [@dynan2012evolution]. The model's earnings panel drops the Latino sample, which the PSID added in 1990 and dropped after 1995 [@psid2025usermanual], because for 1990 to 1996 the panel reads the PSID's core individual weights, which give those records zero weight (`data/panels.py`, `data/family.py`). Every blind test weights its PSID cohort with the PSID's cross-sectional individual weights, and none recalibrates them.

**Attrition.** By 1989, 49 percent of the people interviewed in 1968 were still giving interviews, a count that treats deaths as losses [@fitzgerald1998attrition]. By 2015, on a weighted measure that counts only survivors, the PSID estimates that 40.4 percent of the 1968 sample responded: 41.0 percent of the SRC sample and 33.4 percent of the SEO sample [@chang2023longweights2021]. Fitzgerald, Gottschalk and Moffitt found that attrition through 1989 "is highly selective and is concentrated among lower socioeconomic status individuals," and among people with less stable earnings, marriage and migration histories. They also found that the PSID's cross-sectional representativeness of the non-immigrant population stayed roughly intact over the same years [@fitzgerald1998attrition]. Because the men who stayed had steadier histories than those who left, the authors expected turnover, hazard rates and other second moments to run smaller in the remaining sample than in the population. That instability explains little of who leaves, however, so they judged significant bias in studies of such dynamic outcomes unlikely, and they recommended that researchers check how sensitive their results are to attrition [@fitzgerald1998attrition]. Schoeni and Wiemers find that attrition biases standard estimates of how closely children's incomes follow their parents', and that weights built only on earlier characteristics may not correct it [@schoeni2015attrition].

**Low earnings.** The PSID's documented earnings problems concentrate at the bottom of the distribution. From 1968 to 2007, PSID and CPS family income distributions match fairly closely between the 5th and 95th percentiles and less well in the top and bottom 5 percent [@gouskova2010comparing]. Many of these problems trace to the PSID's move to computer-assisted telephone interviewing and new processing software in 1993 and 1994. PSID staff warned that the change could leave a "double seam" in the income data, and the PSID lacked the staff to re-edit the 1990–1997 data with the editing system it adopted in 2000 [@kim1999incomeplus; @kim2000quality]. The share of household heads recorded with zero labor earnings despite working more than 120 hours in the year jumped right after income year 1991, stayed high through 2002 and fell back in 2004. Dynan, Elmendorf and Sichel judge it a change in measurement, not in the economy [@dynan2012evolution]. Item nonresponse for heads' and wives' labor income rose from about 2 percent in 1980 to over 6 percent in 2001 and 2003 [@killewald2011item]. The PSID's earnings imputation rates run 3 to 4 percent, against recent rates of about 45 percent in the CPS and 49 percent in the Survey of Income and Program Participation [@moffitt2023reconciling]. In its 2007 wave the PSID filled any missing wage it could not impute from job records or the prior wave with the median wage [@duffy2011imputation].

These problems run through the debate over whether American earnings and incomes grew less stable. Hacker and Jacobs, who report that short-term family income variance roughly doubled from 1969 to 2004, acknowledge that the PSID departs from the CPS at the bottom of the income distribution for roughly five years in the mid-1990s, and they find it representative again by the decade's end [@hacker2008rising]. Shin and Solon find little rise in men's earnings volatility through most of the 1990s, a reading they note grows stronger if one discounts observations drawn from the 1993 and 1994 interviews [@shin2008trends]. A 2008 Congressional Budget Office report, which links survey data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation to SSA's earnings records, finds the variability of individual earnings roughly flat since the mid-1980s and repeats Dynan and coauthors' caution about the PSID's early-1990s data [@cbo2008variability]. Gottschalk and Moffitt, by contrast, conclude from cross-sectional comparisons with the CPS that the procedural changes had little effect on trends in the PSID's income distribution [@gottschalk2009rising]. Their comparison covers distributions within each year, while the zero-earnings reports Dynan and coauthors flag show up across a person's consecutive years. PSID staff judged that the income series kept its basic continuity, and they read the PSID's lower incomes at the bottom as possibly more accurate reports of poor families' circumstances [@kim2000quality]. Moffitt and Zhang, examining attrition, item nonresponse, imputation and other features of the PSID, find no evidence that any of them significantly biases its trends in men's earnings volatility [@moffitt2020estimating]. A reconciliation of six survey and administrative sources on men's earnings finds no strong overall trend in volatility among working men since the mid-1980s, and it traces most of the small remaining differences in trends across sources to the left tail of earnings. The PSID has the smallest left tail of the six: about 5 percent of its observations have earnings under $20,000 a year, against about 25 percent in the Census Bureau's Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics records. The most common hypothesis for that gap, the authors write, is that survey respondents often fail to report earnings from short, part-year jobs [@moffitt2023reconciling].

The model reads the PSID's labor income as the PSID records it, imputations included, takes reported zero earnings at face value, and corrects none of these problems. It also carries a break that its own code documents: through income year 1992, heads' labor income includes the labor part of farm and business income, which the PSID records separately from 1993, so earnings windows that straddle 1992 and 1993 mix two concepts (`data/family.py`). No gate tests for these problems. Gate 1 scores zero-earnings spells and transitions against the PSID's own records, so it inherits any error in them. Its benefit-space block scores deciles 3 through 9 of a benefit proxy and, pooled across seeds, the group with no earnings in its anchor year. It only reports the bottom two deciles, because there the discrepancy between two halves of the real PSID alone exceeds the block's 5 percent band. Gate 1 also scores only the years 1998 to 2022 at ages 25 to 59 (`gates.yaml`, gate_1). Recorded earnings before 1997 cover most of the years in the 1968–2010 careers the projection tests read, and the only gate that scores them is gate 2c, which reads them for married couples: who marries whom by earnings and how earnings move around marriage and divorce (`gates.yaml`, gate_2). A sensitivity we report but do not gate drops the 9,286 of 126,867 person-years in gate 1's earnings view that the PSID flags as assigned, and the ten-year autocorrelation of log earnings moves from 0.539 to 0.550 (`runs/imputation_sensitivity_v1.json`). Exercise 2's untested hypotheses for its gap include thinner PSID coverage of low-income unmarried people (@sec-blind).

The model's career construction leaves gaps of its own. Since the move to biennial interviews, the PSID's income questions center on the calendar year before each interview, with at least minimal questions about the "off" year before that [@psid1999familyfile]. The model's main earnings panel reads only the prior-year amounts, so after 1996 it observes earnings every other year and measures two-year changes, never one-year ones (`data/family.py`). Exercise 4 alone reads the off-year reports, for 2001 to 2021 (@sec-coverage). For the 7,486 members of the 2011-wave cohort who reach 62 between 1979 and 2030, about half of the career years through 2010 hold values we imputed or set to zero (@sec-coverage). The imputed years are the odd years from 1997, which the model fills from neighboring years. The years set to zero include years in which the person lived in no responding PSID family, odd years with no recorded neighbor, and income years through 1995 in which the PSID recorded the person's earnings as a family head or spouse but gave the person no weight, as it did for people who married into a PSID family. They also include years in which the person lived in a responding family as neither its head nor a spouse, because the model reads labor income only for heads and spouses (`estimates/career.py`, `data/family.py`).

## What the model does about each limit

The model addresses these limits in two ways, and we plan a third. None removes them.

**Transport onto Microcosm's calibrated frame.** The model is built to project from Microcosm's frame in place of a PSID sample, so that the frame supplies the population's size and makeup and the PSID supplies the transitions. Microcosm calibrates the frame's household weights to administrative totals, among them IRS income statistics, Social Security payments by benefit type and Census population counts by age [@microcosm2026]. Gate w1 applies the processes the model fits on the PSID to every adult in the frame, seeding each adult's marital history from the frame's own married share at ages 25 to 34, and checks 43 cross-sectional cells of the result against the frame: earnings by age and sex, marital shares, spouse coresidence and one household-size share. Gate w1 scores its marital cells at ages 25 to 34 against the same frame values the seeding reads, so those cells are in sample (`models/transport_deployment_v3.py`). The gate reports the rest without scoring them, and it certifies no transition (`gates.yaml`, gate_w1). Any bias in the PSID's transitions, such as the understated turnover that selective attrition can produce, therefore survives the transport. No projection starts from the frame yet; the four blind tests each use a closed PSID cohort with the PSID's own weights.

**Gates scored on the PSID.** The gates that score the model against the PSID set most of their tolerances from the discrepancy between two disjoint halves of the real PSID panel (@sec-scoring). A smaller panel produces a wider floor and a looser tolerance. Gates 2, 2b, 2c, m4 and m6 demote to report-only any cell whose weaker half holds fewer than 20 events or whose tolerance would exceed a cap, ln(1.5) for most cells and 0.15 for gate m6's earnings correlations (`gates.yaml`). These rules price the PSID's sampling noise. They cannot detect a bias that both halves share, because both halves come from the same selected and attrited panel: such a gate tests whether the model reproduces the PSID, and leaves open how far the PSID departs from the population. Gate m6 scores only the people the PSID observed in each later wave, treats the PSID's record of deaths above age 85 as confounded by attrition, and certifies nothing about mortality drift (`gates.yaml`, gate_m6).

**A planned check against administrative earnings records.** We plan to set the earnings careers the model reads from the PSID, and those it generates, against the Social Security Administration's 2006 Earnings Public-Use File. The file holds annual earnings records for 1951 through 2006 from a 1 percent random sample of all Social Security numbers issued before 2007, 4,384,254 people in all [@ssa2011epuf; @ssa2011epufdict].^[SSA's article introducing the file gives 4,348,254 in three places and 4,384,254 in another; its own count of the underlying sample less the records it removed yields 4,384,254 [@compson2011epuf].] Its records come from the earnings posted to workers' Social Security records, so they do not depend on anyone continuing to answer a survey. They hold only earnings up to each year's taxable maximum from jobs Social Security covers, with wages and self-employment combined, and the file records each person's birth year and sex and nothing about marriage, children, disability or death [@compson2011epuf]. The file follows each person across years, so it can test change over time as well as single years. Moffitt and Zhang report that the PSID's earnings data have never been matched to government administrative records [@moffitt2020estimating]. The comparison would run by birth year and sex and cover the share of years with no covered earnings, the share of low-earnings years, movement into and out of covered work, and how persistent a worker's position stays over time. Selective attrition and weak low-end reporting would distort these statistics, and the PSID's own halves cannot reveal the distortion. The comparison has to put the model's earnings on the file's terms, capped at each year's taxable maximum and limited to covered work. It also has to put the two populations on common terms. The file records no deaths, so a run of years without earnings can mean retirement, disability or death [@compson2011epuf], and its sample of Social Security numbers includes the post-1968 immigrants the PSID largely leaves out. The file's own low end is coarse: SSA replaces every amount under $100 with that year's average and rounds amounts from $100 to $1,000 at random to a base of $25 [@ssa2011epufdict; @compson2011epuf]. We registered the rules for one part of this comparison before computing any PSID value on the file's terms, as we do every gate (`docs/amendments/gate_epuf_registration_proposal.md`). That part covers the generated earnings, which overlap the file only in the even years from 1998 to 2004. On that overlap only two cells met the rules for gating, and we found nothing they would catch that gate 1 does not, so we report the comparison without a pass or fail. We have not yet scored the model's earnings against the file, and we have not run the comparison of careers.

| Limit | What it does to the model | What the model does today | What remains open |
|---|---|---|---|
| Size: 4,802 families in 1968 and 9,152 in 2023 | Sampling noise in fitted transitions and in small groups; exercise 2 scores 483 people, 14 of them never married | Gates scored on the PSID set tolerances from its own sampling noise and leave underpowered cells report-only; gate w1 places the PSID's processes on Microcosm's frame, which no projection starts from yet | Sampling error in the fitted transitions |
| Selection: families of 1968 and their descendants, two immigrant refreshers, a 1997 cut that fell mostly on the low-income oversample | Transitions learned from a population defined in 1968 | The PSID's weights; on Microcosm's frame, gate w1 checks the cross-sectional makeup | Transitions of groups the PSID covers thinly |
| Attrition: 49 percent of 1968 members still interviewed in 1989; 40.4 percent of survivors responding in 2015 | Selective attrition can understate turnover and hazard rates | The PSID's weights; gate m6 scores only people the PSID observed | The planned check against SSA's earnings file |
| Low earnings: interviewing and processing changes from 1993, zero-earnings reports through 2002 that Dynan and coauthors attribute to measurement, rising item nonresponse, the smallest left tail of six data sets | Low earners and zero-earnings years carry the most measurement error, and minimum-benefit and poverty results depend on them | No correction; gate 1 scores zero-earnings dynamics only against the PSID's own records and leaves the bottom two benefit-proxy deciles unscored | The planned check against SSA's earnings file |
| Gaps in recorded careers: biennial interviews since 1997 | About half of the career years through 2010 for the 7,486 cohort members who reach 62 between 1979 and 2030 hold imputed or zero values | Fills the odd years after 1996 from neighboring years and sets other missing years to zero | The planned check against SSA's earnings file |

: The PSID's limits, what each does to the model, what the model does about it today and what remains open. {#tbl-psid-limits}

# What remains to build {#sec-remaining}

Forward earnings are the largest piece the projection tests still lack. The forward earnings law passes its own gate, m6, and no projection test uses it yet. To compare the model with DYNASIM3's reform results, we need projections that begin in 2010, end in 2030 and turn on people aged 60 to 69. The law does not yet reach those people in their sixties. Ages 60 to 64 sit inside its fitted range of 25 to 64, but the projection cohort starts in 2010, four years before the law's 2014 boundary, and above 64 the law has no fitted distribution. We plan first to connect forward earnings to the projection tests, and then to build the benefit mechanics that depend on earnings. Each step is a design that joins the model only after it passes a dedicated registered gate, and none has joined yet. Two pieces already exist: the retirement earnings test parameters, and the code for a planned rerun of both projection tests, which we have merged into the repository.

**Forward earnings in the projection.** We plan to carry the earnings state of a 2010 cohort forward to 2014, the law's fitted boundary. A new transport gate would score those carried-forward earnings states against the PSID's 2012 and 2014 waves. We already used those two waves to select the model, and the gate's registration would say so. We would also fit a second version of the law on a wider age range, 25 to 69, with one gate for each of three age bands: 62–64, 65–66 and 67–69. Any 2030 claim that rests on forward earnings would need evidence from a planned backtest that uses 2006 as its boundary year and spans the PSID waves from 2006 to 2022. That backtest could not support a 2030 claim alone, because those same waves already shaped our modeling choices. We would record three separate monthly series from 2010 through 2030: labor earnings, covered earnings and the earnings that count under the retirement earnings test.

**The retirement earnings test.** The earnings test's parameters agree with SSA's published history. No projection applies them yet, and we plan to apply them next. An annual ledger would track entitlement, provisional suspension, final deduction and the grace year, and we would validate it against SSA's worked examples. One separate module would make the adjustment at full retirement age for the months in which the earnings test withheld benefits. Another would recompute benefits when later earnings arrive. One of three untested hypotheses for exercise 3's largest gap, 4.22 percentage points at ages 65 to 69, is an earnings test extended to age 68. Once we combine the earnings-test machinery with fixed claiming, we could test that hypothesis for the first time.

**Gross benefits and dual entitlement.** A gross-benefit layer would add the family maximum, age reductions, dual-entitlement reductions and the monthly family payment. We would check it against statutory worked examples, and against Axiom only where a pinned rule exists. A separate rerun, which we plan to register, would repeat both projection tests, exercises 1 and 3, with statutory computation years for disability benefits and with dual entitlement for disability and spouse benefits. We have merged its code into the repository, and so far we have tested it only on invented data. It has no registration yet, and because it comes after the published results, we label it post hoc.

**Claiming.** The engine draws claim ages from a fixed distribution, and no claim age responds to a reform. We plan to replace that distribution with a monthly claiming hazard, which we would estimate on the insured population that has not yet claimed. We would also add a claiming response identified from policy variation, but only if the data we can access permit a credible design. Even then, to model a claiming response to a full retirement age of 68, we would have to extrapolate past every policy anyone has observed.

**Family and population in the projection.** The family models pass their gates, 2, 2b and 2c, but none runs inside a projection test yet. We plan to combine the gated marriage and divorce models with the widowhood that a spouse's death already triggers in the projection tests. We would redraw initial states and declare which populations the projection covers. A registered projection gate would score the result, and a joint validation would check the earnings, claiming, disability, payment and survivor pathways together. In the projection, entrants, both births and immigrants, stay report-only until we admit into the model a way of setting starting states that supports them.

**Axiom execution.** Axiom reproduces the Python oracle's AIME for all 7,486 people we tested, and so far it reproduces nothing else. Axiom's Social Security encodings await acceptance, which must come before the full benefit rules can run in Axiom. We plan to extend Axiom from AIME onward through the PIA, auxiliary benefits and the earnings test.

**Wealth, pensions and the long horizon.** The model reads PSID wealth and annuitizes it for income measures, and it projects no wealth. The projection tests end in 2030. Any projection we run well past that year carries one more limit: gate m6 certifies nothing about mortality drift.

**Held-out targets.** We plan two more blind tests under the same protocol as the four existing ones. The first covers the 1946–55 birth cohort from the 2004 report behind exercise 2 [@butrica2004boomers], and its DYNASIM3 values already sit under the existing seal, away from the model's builders. For this test, we would carry the PSID income and wealth mappings forward into the 2015–2023 waves. The second covers the progressive price indexing option, from the 2010 figure behind exercises 1 and 3 [@urban2010detailsmatter]. The report behind that figure omits the option's operational formula, so we would need to register conventions for it. We will run no blind test that needs a projected population until the planned projection gates pass.

**Comparisons beyond DYNASIM.** We plan three comparisons with sources outside DYNASIM, and none is yet registered or run. The first sets the change in total 2030 benefits, from a projection re-timed to each provision's start date, against the 2030 cost effect that OACT and PWBM each publish for the same provision texts [@ssa2026oact; @pwbm2026provisions]. OACT's one-point COLA cut from December 2027 is the primary row. OACT's two schedules that raise the FRA to 68, starting with people who turn 62 in 2027, are secondary rows. OACT prints its effects as percentages of taxable payroll to two decimal places, which suffices for the COLA row. By 2030 the FRA schedules reach only people who turned 62 in 2027 or later, so their effects may not register at two decimals. PWBM's CSV files serve as the primary comparator for those rows; the one PWBM file we checked for precision, from a payroll-tax provision, stores its values at full precision. Arithmetic on the COLA text alone should land close to OACT's and PWBM's values for that row, because the cut gives everyone eligible before 2028 the same three reduced increases, those of December 2027, 2028 and 2029. We plan to report that calculation beside the model's result. The second sets the model's 2030 benefit changes by age against SSA's archived MINT5 tables for a one-point COLA cut and an FRA of 68, against MINT8's FRA of 68 and against PWBM's two FRA-68 grids [@ssa2011mint5cola; @ssa2011mint5fra68; @ssa2024mintoptions; @pwbm2026provisions]. Each of these needs a projection run re-timed to that source's schedule. MINT5's COLA cut starts in 2011, against the increase effective December 2009 (first paid in January 2010) in the model's primary row. MINT5's FRA reaches 68 for people turning 62 in 2038, against 2022 in the model. MINT reports medians where the model reports a ratio of means. The MINT8 and PWBM schedules start in 2024 and 2027, so by 2030 they reach only the youngest beneficiaries. PWBM's grids cover ages 62 to 75 in 2030, and their caption says some changes before 70 can come from delayed claiming, while the model's primary FRA row holds claiming fixed. The same set adds MINT8's reconfigured minimum benefit by sex, whose share of beneficiaries with a higher benefit is only a proxy for the share receiving a minimum. The third uses CBO where its precision allows [@cbo2015ssoptions; @cbo2024deficitoptions]. CBO's 2015 workbook stores every value as a percentage of GDP to one decimal place, so its FRA-68 option can check at most the direction of the 2030 change. CBO's 2024 FRA-70 option enters at its fiscal-2030 column, which sets a fiscal year against a calendar year. Every one of these tables is public, so these tests can be blind only in procedure: we plan to seal each comparator's pages from the people who build the model's runs. Agreement would bear on the composition of 2030 benefits and on COLA mechanics. It would not test long-run dynamics. The model's repository also holds one check against a source outside DYNASIM that we registered but did not run blind. It sets the model's cost ordering of four benefit reductions against CBO's 2005 estimates as @mermin2005benefitreductions reports them, and our registered ordering forecast did not hold. The committed artifact labels those CBO estimates as DYNASIM3, and an erratum in the repository corrects the label [@microcosm2026issue488].

# The landscape of Social Security models {#sec-related}

SSA's actuaries project what Social Security reforms do to the trust funds. SSA's research office, the Urban Institute and the Penn Wharton Budget Model (PWBM) project reforms' effects with dynamic microsimulation. CBO publishes its own reform estimates, and its long-term model, CBOLT, contains a microsimulation [@cbo2018]. An outsider can download result tables from all five. CBOLT's code is not among CBO's public repositories, and no source we read shows code for the actuaries' projections, SSA's MINT, Urban's DYNASIM or PWBM. CBO does publish a separate 10-year trust fund model in Excel, which projects OASI and DI balances consistent with CBO's February 2026 baseline [@cbo2026trustfundmodel]. Besides Microcosm Dynamics, we found public code for two other models built to estimate reforms across a population: OG-USA, an overlapping-generations model of the whole economy, and the Cato Institute's model. Household-adequacy models at Morningstar, EBRI, Boston College's Center for Retirement Research and Vanguard project whether households will have enough to retire on. @tbl-landscape lists each model, who runs it, what it opens to outsiders and which reforms it has published results for.

| National Retirement Risk Index (NRRI) | Center for Retirement Research at Boston College | Household adequacy | Code not checked. Figure data as XLSX | Share of working-age households at risk | None |
| Retirement Readiness Model (VRRM) | Vanguard | Household adequacy | Code not checked. Report PDF | Share on track; spending gap or surplus | None |
| Future Elderly Model | USC Schaeffer Center | Demographic simulation | Not checked | Present value of benefits relative to wealth, top and bottom income quintiles | An early eligibility age of 64, an NRA of 70, a smaller COLA, cuts to the top PIA factor (National Academies, 2015) [@nas2015growinggap] |
| Taxes and Growth (TAG) | Tax Foundation | Tax general equilibrium | The overview mentions no public code [@taxfoundationtag2025] | 10-year revenue and deficit; macroeconomic aggregates; after-tax income by quintile | Three payroll-tax options [@taxfoundation2026option44] |
| Seven models in CBO's 2018 symposium | CBO, with the Diamond-Zodrow, EY QUEST, Global Gaidar, JCT, OG-USA and PWBM models | Overlapping generations | Not checked, except OG-USA (CC0-1.0) | Macroeconomic effects | A one-third OASI cut from 2031 [@phillips2019olg; @nelson2019olg] |
| Reformer; BPC plans | Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget; Bipartisan Policy Center | Derived from OACT | — | Trust fund measures | The Reformer's option menu; plans OACT scored [@crfb2025reformer] |
| Open Social Security | Mike Piper | One-household claiming calculator | Code under MIT | Best claiming ages for one household | None; users can apply an across-the-board cut from a year they set [@piper2026opensocialsecurity] |
| Microcosm Dynamics | PolicyEngine | Dynamic microsimulation | Code, estimates and tests under MIT | 2030 benefit changes by age group; poverty at 67; share on a minimum benefit, by sex | The four DYNASIM3 test reforms (@sec-blind); reported, not gated runs of other reforms in the repository |

: Models that estimate US Social Security reforms: who runs each, what an outsider can obtain, what it publishes and which reforms it has published results for. "Not checked" marks a point that no source we read establishes. {#tbl-landscape tbl-colwidths="[13,12,11,17,20,27]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary (OACT) publishes trust fund measures for every provision it scores, and the provision pages we read carry no distributional results. For each provision, OACT publishes a summary of its effect on the 75-year actuarial balance and a single-year table of cost rates, income rates, annual balances and trust fund ratios [@ssa2026oact]. It prints the rates and balances as percentages of current-law taxable payroll, to two decimal places. The tables run from 2026 to 2101 for provisions on the 2026 Trustees Report basis, and categories B, D, E, F and J remain on the 2025 basis. OACT has also scored whole plans in 193 letters, and option sets for the Social Security Advisory Board and NASI [@ssa2026oactletters; @ssa2005oactssab; @ssa2009oactnasi]. CRFB's Reformer builds most of its annual effects from OACT's figures, and BPC takes its reform numbers from OACT's letters, so neither adds an independent estimate [@crfb2025reformer]. CBO's long-term model, CBOLT, has four components: demographic, microsimulation, long-term budget and policy growth. Its microsimulation starts from a 10 percent subsample of SSA's Continuous Work History Sample and keeps the links between spouses, parents and children [@cbo2018]. CBO publishes trust fund and budget measures beside distributional tables by 10-year birth cohort and lifetime household earnings quintile, whose retired-worker tables assume that every worker claims at 65 [@cbo2026longterm]. CBO's reform results appear in options volumes from 2010 and 2015, a 2019 tool with 288 combinations of options and its deficit-reduction volumes [@cbo2010ssoptions; @cbo2015ssoptions; @cbo2019sstool; @cbo2024deficitoptions].

SSA's research office publishes MINT8 tables for 19 reform options [@ssa2024mintoptions]. The Urban Institute, which runs DYNASIM, documents MINT's methods in its final report on MINT8 [@smith2021mint8]. MINT8 runs on Social Security's administrative records matched to the Survey of Income and Program Participation, under the 2023 Trustees Report's assumptions [@ssa2024mint]. Each option comes with 20 tables: benefits, payroll taxes, household income and poverty in 2030, 2050 and 2070, and benefit-to-tax ratios and replacement rates for four birth cohorts from 1960–69 to 2020–29 [@ssa2024mintguide]. SSA's briefs describe MINT's policy comparisons as static, with no behavioral response, and MINT projects a single claiming age [@olsen2008cola; @ssa2024mint]. Tables from MINT5 to MINT7, published by SSA's former Office of Retirement Policy, survive only in the Internet Archive [@ssa2011mint5cola; @ssa2011mint5fra68]. Urban's DYNASIM3 produced the results behind all four blind tests (@sec-blind). DYNASIM4, the current generation, scored five Democratic campaign plans in 2020 and the minimum benefits in three reform proposals in 2021 [@urban2024dynasim4; @smith2020fivedem; @steuerle2021firstthings]. Four Urban repositories on GitHub publish 2017 DYNASIM output, naming no version: incomes for people 62 and older by decade from 2015 to 2065, and trust fund measures by option [@urban2018dynasimshiny1; @urban2018dynasimshiny2; @urban2018dynasimshiny3; @urban2018dynasimcomparisons].

PWBM scores 115 individual provisions in its 2026 release, keyed to OACT's codes where one exists, and it uses OACT's 2026 texts verbatim for the COLA and retirement-age categories [@pwbm2026provisions]. Its 2018 documentation describes a microsimulation that generates earnings, marriages, divorces, children, retirement and death from 1996, with earlier earnings matched from SSA's 2006 Earnings Public Use File [@gokhale2018pwbmss]. PWBM publishes each provision as CSV files: annual trust fund series, and a benefit grid by birth year from 1955 to 2015, age from 62 to 99 and own-lifetime-earnings quintile. The one file we checked for precision, from a payroll-tax provision, stores its values at full precision.

The Cato Institute's model includes a person-level OASI microsimulation and, on a separate branch of its repository, a Python replica of the Trustees' 2025 intermediate projections [@catossmodel2026]. The microsimulation, written in R, starts from 10,000 households in the 2007 CPS. A drift factor in the replica's benefit growth keeps its cost and income rates close to the Trustees'. The model's README says the person-level baseline needs SSA's 2006 public-use earnings file loaded into a database that users build themselves. Cato lists 17 options it offers to score, each with the direction of its effect on spending or revenue and no magnitude [@cato2026menu].

Overlapping-generations and other general-equilibrium models report what a reform does to the economy and the federal budget. OG-Core, with its US calibration OG-USA, is a deterministic general-equilibrium model with perfect foresight, 80 annual ages and 10 lifetime-income groups at each age [@ogcore2026; @ogusa2026]. Jason DeBacker of the Open Research Group ran OG-Core for CRFB's 2026 study of three ways to index a benefit cap [@crfb2026sixfigure]. CBO's 2018 symposium compared seven overlapping-generations models, OG-USA and PWBM's among them, under a one-third cut to OASI benefits in 2031, and reported macroeconomic effects only [@phillips2019olg; @nelson2019olg]. The Tax Foundation's Taxes and Growth model, which joins a tax simulator to a neoclassical production function and an allocation model, scores payroll-tax options for 10-year revenue and macroeconomic effects [@taxfoundationtag2025; @taxfoundation2026option44].

OG-Core's default US-style pension computes a group-level AIME from steady-state earnings, applies three PIA brackets with a cap and an optional floor, and moves benefits with the current wage. That pension leaves out COLAs, claiming choice, early reduction and delayed credits, the earnings test, and disability, spousal and survivor benefits. Neither repository has a trust fund variable, OG-Core has no poverty measure, and OG-USA's payroll revenue includes Medicare's hospital insurance tax. In OG-USA, a uniform benefit cut and a payroll-tax change are parameter changes, and a COLA change needs new code. We reported in OG-Core issue #1234 that the benefit-adjustment parameter, which carries a uniform cut, enters twice into households' saving and labor choices on the time path, the years the model solves before it reaches its steady state [@ogcore2026issue1234]. Our reproduction runs OG-Core's own functions without a full model solve. A higher FRA enters only approximately: as a later benefit start in whole years, whose timing can differ between households' choices and the model's aggregates [@ogcore2026issue1235], or as a phased cut through the benefit-adjustment parameter. A minimum benefit can enter only as a floor on group PIAs.

Among the household-adequacy models, we found published Social Security reform scenarios only from EBRI's Retirement Security Projection Model, which has run proportional benefit cuts in five briefs from 2010 to 2025 [@ebri2026rspm; @vanderhei2010rrr; @copeland2025replacement]. These models report funded ratios, readiness ratings and replacement rates. Morningstar's MMURO runs each household in the Survey of Consumer Finances through 1,000 scenarios to age 120, with a health-state model built on the Health and Retirement Study and Social Security benefits estimated from each member's wage history [@look2024mmuroappendix]. Morningstar's FAQ says the model will not be open for public use [@morningstar2024mmurofaq], and we found no Social Security reform results published from it. In September 2026 MMURO's co-developer Jack VanDerhei argued that scorers should judge reform packages by what they do to household retirement outcomes as well as to trust fund balances [@vanderhei2026ssreform]. Boston College's National Retirement Risk Index projects a replacement rate at 65 for households aged 30 to 59 and compares it with a target [@yin2023nrri; @yin2024nrri], and Vanguard's model assumes scheduled benefits continue [@vanguard2025outlook]. The USC Schaeffer Center describes its Future Elderly Model as a demographic simulation model [@usc2016femgao]. The model gave the National Academies the present value of benefits relative to wealth in the top and bottom income quintiles under six Social Security options [@nas2015growinggap]. At the scale of one household, Open Social Security, an MIT-licensed calculator, finds the best claiming ages and can apply an across-the-board cut from a year the user sets [@piper2026opensocialsecurity].

Outside US Social Security, SimPaths models the life course with open code, and LIAM2 and OpenM++ are open platforms for building dynamic microsimulation models [@bronka2025simpaths; @dementen2014liam2; @openmpp2026]. Destinie 2 and microWELT model pensions and transfers in aging European populations [@blanchet2010destinie; @spielauer2020microwelt]. The dynamic microsimulation literature [@harding1990; @li2013] includes methods for weighting a dynamic model's population [@dekkerscumpston2012] and for aligning simulated outcomes to external totals [@li2014].

We publish distributional outputs from Microcosm Dynamics: 2030 benefit changes by age group, poverty at 67, and the share of beneficiaries on a minimum benefit by sex. The model extends PolicyEngine's open cross-sectional microdata with a longitudinal layer that we estimate on the PSID [@policyengine2026; @ghenis2024]. It produces no cost estimates. The dollar sums in its repository are frame-relative or interim, and none certifies a national level. The model computes no actuarial balance and no trust fund depletion date. We can therefore set it against the trust fund tables of OACT, CBO and PWBM only where those tables convert to a change in one year's total benefits. The model's closest comparators are the other dynamic microsimulations. SSA's archived MINT5 tables for 2030 share the 2008 Trustees assumptions of the model's projection tests, and PWBM scores OACT's own 2026 COLA and retirement-age texts verbatim. We plan no comparison with the adequacy models, whose measures the model does not produce, or with the overlapping-generations models or Cato's model. The comparisons we plan use tables from OACT, PWBM, MINT and CBO (@sec-remaining).
